# Jacek Karpiński — Polish Computer Engineer and Innovator
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish engineer known for his significant contributions to early computing and computer engineering. Despite severe wartime injuries and involvement in the Polish resistance during WWII, he pursued studies in electrical engineering and quickly gained recognition. His early work included the Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics (AAH, 1957) and AKAT-1 (1959), the world’s first transistor-based differential equations analyzer. Karpiński earned a UNESCO scholarship, allowing him to visit major US labs and meet notable scientists like Claude Shannon; however, he chose to return to Poland, continuing his pioneering work.
Karpiński developed multiple innovative machines in Poland: a perceptron (1964), one of the earliest in the world; the high-speed KAR-65 computer (1968), and most notably the K-202 minicomputer (1973), which used Intel 4004 chips and featured memory segmentation with paging, modularity, and remarkable speed rivaling Western counterparts. Despite technological excellence, K-202 faced administrative hurdles and political opposition, never achieving mass production. Karpiński was also involved in cooperative activity with Polish intelligence, gathering technical data abroad. Later in life, he worked in Switzerland, attempted business ventures, and was posthumously honored for his achievements. Karpiński’s legacy remains debated, but his engineering ingenuity and vision marked a significant chapter in Polish computer history.
